claim: A large Cochrane systematic review of randomized trials found that offering general health checks to unselected adults has little or no effect on all-cause or cancer mortality and probably little or no effect on cardiovascular mortality, despite increasing some diagnoses; this is a high-certainty example where a plausible preventive-health intervention does not translate into better major outcomes.

source.title: General health checks for reducing illness and mortality

study_characteristics.design_note: The review compared invitations to one or more general health checks for adults not selected for a particular disease or risk factor with no invitation. Risk of bias was generally low for the primary outcomes.

key_results: All-cause mortality: RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.03; high-certainty evidence.
Cancer mortality: RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.12; high-certainty evidence.
Cardiovascular mortality: RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.16; moderate-certainty evidence.
Fatal and non-fatal ischaemic heart disease: RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.03; high-certainty evidence.
The review reports that health checks increased the number of new diagnoses in some trials, while evidence on several possible harms and downstream procedures was incomplete.
why_high_information_value: HumanityAI currently has little direct preventive-health intervention evidence, while health checks are intuitively appealing and widely understandable.
The finding separates detection activity from patient-important outcomes: more diagnoses do not necessarily imply lower mortality or morbidity.
The large randomized evidence base makes this a useful calibration case for resisting surrogate-outcome and activity-count bias in future recommendations.
limitations: The review was published in 2019 and many underlying trials are older; contemporary targeted prevention, risk-stratified screening, and disease-specific screening should not be inferred to be ineffective from this evidence.
The intervention is a broad package of general health checks rather than one standardized protocol, and delivery differed across trials and health systems.

The review mainly addresses population-level invitations for general checks among adults not selected for specific risk factors; it does not apply to symptom-driven evaluation or recommended screening for particular diseases or high-risk groups.
Evidence on some harms, follow-up procedures, psychological effects, and resource use was incomplete, so the record should not claim a precise net-harm estimate.
A mortality null does not prove no benefit for every intermediate or quality-of-life outcome, and the review did not establish cost-effectiveness across current healthcare systems.
This evidence does not establish HumanityAI's comparative advantage in healthcare policy or imply a recommendation to stop clinically indicated preventive care.
counterevidence_and_uncertainty: Health checks can increase detection of conditions and risk factors, which may be valuable in some targeted contexts even though the pooled general-check strategy did not improve major mortality outcomes.

Changes in modern preventive treatments and screening practices may alter the value of specific components, so any current policy use should distinguish broad general checks from evidence-based targeted prevention.
recommended_integration: After independent source verification, add a normal P03 intervention-evidence record emphasizing the distinction between diagnostic activity and patient-important outcomes. Do not generalize the result to targeted screening, symptom-driven care, or high-risk populations.
